pages.p:
C++ is a programming language. A program is a list of instructions for the computer.

C++ is fast. It is used to build games, web browsers, music software, and parts of phones and cars. Many other languages borrow ideas from it, so learning C++ teaches you how computers really work.

In this course you will write small programs and see what they print.

You write C++ in a text file. That text is called **source code**. A computer cannot run source code directly.

A tool called a **compiler** reads your source code and translates it into a **program** the computer can run. This step is called **compiling**.

So the steps are:
• write the source code
• compile it
• run the program
pages.tip: If the compiler finds a mistake, it stops and tells you. No program is made until the mistakes are fixed.

pages.p: This is the smallest useful C++ program. It prints one line of text. Do not worry about every word yet. The next page explains each part.

• «#include <iostream>» brings in the tools for input and output.
• «using namespace std;» lets you write «cout» instead of the longer «std::cout».
• «int main()» is where the program starts. Everything between «{ }» runs, from top to bottom.
• «cout << ...» prints.
• «return 0;» says: the program finished fine.
pages.tip: In «main», «return 0;» is optional. If you leave it out, C++ adds it for you.

pages.p:
«cout» is the screen (the name means "console output"). The arrows «<<» push things into it. Text goes between double quotes. The quotes are not printed.

«endl» ends the line, like pressing Enter.
You can chain many pieces with «<<» in one statement. C++ adds **no spaces** for you, so put them inside the text yourself.
pages.tip: Spaces inside quotes are printed. Spaces between « << » pieces are not.

pages.p:
There are two ways to start a new line. «endl» is a word you chain. «"\n"» is a special symbol inside the text. The «\n» is one character that means "new line".

Without either of them, the next «cout» continues on the same line.
pages.tip: Both «endl» and «\n» work for beginners. «\n» is slightly faster, «endl» is easier to read.

pages.p: Numbers do not need quotes. A sum is worked out before it is printed. Text in quotes is never calculated.
A **comment** is a note for humans. The compiler ignores it. Use «//» for a one-line comment and «/* ... */» for a longer one.
pages.tip: Putting «//» in front of a line is a quick way to switch it off while you test.

pages.p:
Each instruction is a **statement**. In C++ every statement must end with a semicolon «;». It works like the full stop in a sentence.

A program runs top to bottom, one statement after another. The line «#include ...» is special. It has no semicolon.
pages.tip: Forgetting a «;» is the most common beginner mistake. Everybody does it.

pages.p:
C++ is **case-sensitive**. «cout» works. «Cout» and «COUT» do not. The same is true for «main» and «endl».

Text needs a closing quote, and every «{» needs a «}». Round brackets, quotes and curly brackets always come in pairs.

Spaces and new lines between statements do not matter to the compiler. Use them to make your code easy to read.
pages.tip: When you get an error, first check spelling, capital letters, quotes, brackets and semicolons.

pages.p:
If the code breaks the rules, the compiler prints an **error message** and no program is made. A message looks like this:

«main.cpp:5:30: error: expected ';' before 'cout'»

Read it in parts: the file, the **line number** (5), then what is wrong. The compiler often notices a missing «;» only when it reaches the next line, so also look at the line just above the one it names.
pages.tip: Always fix the first error first. Later errors are often just echoes of it.

pages.p:
The real name of «cout» is «std::cout». «std» is the standard library, and «::» means "inside". The line «using namespace std;» lets you skip the «std::» part.

Both programs below do the same thing. In this course we use «using namespace std;» because it is shorter.

hand.ans: It translates your source code into a program the computer can run
wrong: It runs your code one word at a time and never makes a file
It checks that your comments are written in correct English
It makes your code shorter so it runs faster
hand.why: The compiler turns source code into a program. If it finds a mistake, it reports an error instead.
The pieces are printed one after another. The space is inside the second piece of text, so it appears.

hand.q: Which line do you need to use «cout»?
hand.why: The header «iostream» holds «cout» and «endl». You include it with «#include <iostream>», and no semicolon.
«endl» ends the line after each statement, so B starts on a new line.
«<<» sends the text towards «cout». The arrows point at the screen.
Without «endl» or «\n», the second «cout» continues on the same line.

hand.q: Put the lines in order to make a working program.
hand.why: The include and the using line come first. Then «main» holds the code that runs.

hand.q: Which one is a valid comment?
hand.why: In C++ a one-line comment starts with «//». The «#» symbol is used for lines like «#include».
«\n» inside text is the new-line character. It is not printed as two symbols.
Every statement in C++ ends with a semicolon.

hand.q: Where does a C++ program start running?
hand.ans: At the first line inside main()
wrong: At the first line of the file
At the last line of the file
hand.why: Programs always start in «main». The «#include» lines only prepare the tools.
The line starting with «//» is a comment. The compiler ignores it.

hand.q: The compiler says «expected ';' before 'cout'». What most likely happened?
hand.ans: A semicolon is missing at the end of the line above
wrong: The word cout is spelled with a capital C
The program has no main function
The text has no closing quote
hand.why: The compiler only notices a missing semicolon when the next statement begins, so look at the previous line.

hand.q: Complete the name of the function where every C++ program starts.
hand.why: The function «main» is the starting point of every C++ program.

hard.why: Text in quotes is printed as written. Without quotes, the sum is calculated first.
Each «\n» starts a new line, so no «endl» is needed.

hard.q: The compiler reports an error for this program. How do you fix it?
hard.ans: Add a semicolon at the end of the line that prints One
wrong: Remove endl from the line that prints One
Add a comma between the two cout lines
hard.why: The statement printing «One» is not finished. It needs «;». The compiler points at line 5 because it only notices there.
Two «endl» in a row end the line and then add an empty line before B.

hard.q: What is the job of «using namespace std;»?
hard.ans: It lets you write cout and endl instead of std::cout and std::endl
wrong: It loads the tools for input and output
It tells the compiler where main starts
It makes capital letters and small letters the same
hard.why: The tools come from «#include <iostream>». The using line only saves you from typing «std::» each time.

wrong: Nothing, because there is no using namespace std;
hard.why: With the full names «std::cout» and «std::endl», the «using» line is not needed.
Everything between «/*» and «*/» is a comment, even when it spans several lines.

hard.q: Which line makes the compiler complain?
wrong: No line: the compiler ignores capital letters
hard.why: C++ is case-sensitive. «Cout» with a capital C is an unknown name. Line 4 uses the right spelling.

hard.q: Put the lines in order to print a countdown.
hard.why: The lines inside «main» run from top to bottom, so the output follows their order.

hard.q: Complete the code so it prints Hi and Bye on two lines.
hard.why: Putting «endl» or «"\n"» between the two words starts a new line there.

items.why: The statement that prints Hello is missing its semicolon.

items.symptom: The compiler complains about «>>» and no program is made.
items.why: The arrows must point towards cout: «cout <<». The arrows «>>» are for input.

items.symptom: fatal error: iostrem: No such file or directory
items.why: The header is called «iostream». A misspelled name cannot be found.

items.symptom: It prints HelloWorld on one line, but two lines were expected.
items.why: Without «endl» or «\n», the next output continues on the same line.

items.symptom: The program does not link: undefined reference to «main».
items.why: C++ looks for a function named «main» in small letters. «Main» is a different name.

items.symptom: It prints «Line A/nLine B» on one line instead of two lines.
items.why: The new-line symbol is a backslash: «\n». A slash «/n» is just two normal characters.

project.title: My First Banner
project.brief:
Write a program that prints this exact text. It does not read any input.

«=== My First Program ===»
«Hello, world!»
«I am learning C++.»
«Bye!»

Sample run:

Input: (none)
Output:
=== My First Program ===
Hello, world!
I am learning C++.
Bye!

Put each line on its own line with «cout» and «endl» (or «\n»).

samples.out:
=== My First Program ===
Hello, world!
I am learning C++.
Bye!

tests.label: Prints the greeting and the other lines
